lessons.title: Choosing a Peer Set and Reading Historical Valuation Bands on screener.in

children.text: Every relative valuation rests on a benchmark: "cheap compared with what?" The two benchmarks Indian investors use most are a company's peers and its own history, and screener.in puts both a click away, with a peer comparison table on every company page and ten years of valuation charts. That convenience is also the danger. An automatically generated peer list and a ten-year median line look authoritative, but both can be badly wrong for the stock in front of you. This lesson shows you how to build benchmarks you can trust.

body.text: A multiple is only as good as its benchmark. True peers share economics, not just an industry label. A company's own history is only a fair benchmark if the business, its growth prospects and interest rates have not fundamentally changed.

children.text: Part 1: Choosing a Peer Set
A
peer set
should contain companies whose multiples would move for the same reasons as your company's. That means matching on the drivers of value from Chapter 1, not on the name of the industry.

markDefs.definition: A group of listed companies with similar business economics, such as growth, margins, returns, risk and capital intensity, used as a benchmark for relative valuation.

body.caption: What a true peer should share

cells: Different models earn different returns and carry different risks
A domestic branded pharma company compared with a US generics exporter
Faster growth justifies a higher multiple, if returns are high
A mature two-wheeler maker compared with an EV-focused startup
Higher ROCE means less reinvestment per rupee of growth
A 30% ROCE paint company compared with a 12% ROCE one
A net-cash cement company compared with a heavily indebted one on P/E
Small, thinly traded stocks often trade at a discount
A ₹2,000 crore small cap compared with a Nifty 50 leader
Peak or trough earnings distort multiples
A sugar company in a record-price year compared with one in a normal year
Consolidated vs standalone, Ind AS 116 treatment
Standalone P/E for one company, consolidated for another

body.text: The peer comparison table on screener.in is built from broad industry classifications. It is a useful starting list, never a finished peer set. "Pharmaceuticals" can include domestic branded formulations, US generics exporters, API manufacturers, contract research and CDMO businesses, each with very different growth, margins and multiples. "IT" mixes large services firms, mid-tier specialists, engineering services and product companies.

children.text: Worked Example: The Misleading Industry Median

Deccan Generics Ltd is a fictional NSE-listed pharma company that earns most of its revenue selling generic medicines in the United States. It trades at ₹1,200, 24× earnings, with 6% expected earnings growth and a 13% ROCE. Its screener.in peer table, based on the pharmaceuticals industry label, lists nine companies.

stats.label: Median P/E, US generics exporters only

children.text: Against the full industry list, Deccan Generics Ltd appears to trade at a 40% discount, and a quick screen would call it undervalued. Against the three companies that actually share its business model, growth and returns, it trades at a 20% premium. The domestic branded companies deserve higher multiples because they grow faster and earn roughly double the ROCE. The CDMO and contract research companies carry growth expectations Deccan does not have. Same industry label, completely different conclusion.

body.label: Median, not average
body.context: Here the median (40.0×) and average (38.4×) happen to be close, but with peers spanning 18× to 72×, one more extreme multiple could drag the average far from the typical peer. The median is robust to that. Also exclude loss-making companies, whose P/E is negative or meaningless. The exercise at the end of this lesson shows the gap in action.

children.text: Where to find better peers
Annual reports and earnings calls:
management often names the competitors it tracks.
IPO offer documents:

the "Basis for Offer Price" section of a DRHP or RHP compares the issuer with listed peers it considers comparable. Treat it as a starting point, since issuers have an incentive to choose flattering peers.
Segment disclosures:
for diversified companies, compare each segment with its own pure-play peers.
Global peers:
for export-heavy businesses, listed global competitors can be relevant, adjusting for country risk and interest rates.

body.text: When no peer is a perfect match, which is almost always, do not force a single median. Compare your company with each close peer on growth, ROCE and margins, and explain why it deserves a higher or lower multiple. A premium or discount you can justify is worth far more than a median you cannot.

children.text: Part 2: Reading Historical Valuation Bands

The second benchmark is the company's own past. screener.in's chart section lets you plot a company's P/E ratio over time, with its median over the chosen period, and similar charts for other valuation ratios such as price to book and EV/EBITDA. A stock trading well below its historical median looks cheap. A
valuation band
shows how unusual the current level really is.

markDefs.definition: A range around a company's historical average or median multiple, often drawn at plus and minus one standard deviation, used to judge whether the current multiple is unusually high or low relative to its own history.

children.text: Konark Paints Ltd is a fictional listed decorative paints maker. Its year-end P/E over the last ten years, with the median and a one standard deviation band calculated excluding the distorted FY21 figure, is below. Current EPS is ₹60.

body.title: Konark Paints: year-end P/E and historical band (illustrative)
Show me how the band is calculated

children.text: Excluding FY21, the nine year-end P/Es are 48, 55, 58, 52, 74, 62, 60, 50, 44.
Median: the middle value when sorted = 55.0×.
Mean: sum ÷ 9 = 55.9×.
Standard deviation: the square root of the average squared distance from the mean (using n - 1) = 9.0×.
In Excel, use =MEDIAN(range), =AVERAGE(range) and =STDEV.S(range).
At 44×, Konark Paints sits below its historical band. Applying the median would suggest ₹3,300, about 25% upside. Before believing that, ask why the multiple has fallen.

body.text: FY21 shows why raw history misleads. In the pandemic year, earnings fell sharply while the share price recovered quickly, sending the P/E to 88×. That spike was about a temporary drop in "E", not a change in how the market valued the business. Including it lifts the median and widens the band. Remove or adjust such years before drawing conclusions.

children.text: Why the Past Multiple May Not Return

body.caption: Five reasons a historical band can be the wrong benchmark

cells: Industry returns and growth expectations fall
A well-funded conglomerate enters decorative paints, pricing aggressively to win dealers
The company is larger and its market more mature
Volume growth slows from mid-teens to high single digits
A higher risk-free rate lowers every justified multiple
The 10-year G-sec yield is higher than in the years that set the median
Raw material costs rise and dealer incentives increase
A rerating that was itself excessive
The historical period included a bubble
Multiples in an earlier boom were never justified by fundamentals

children.text: One more comparison helps separate company-specific change from market-wide mood: the
relative P/E
against the Nifty 50.

markDefs.definition: A stock's P/E divided by the P/E of a benchmark index such as the Nifty 50. It shows whether a stock's premium or discount to the market has changed over time.

body.title: Konark Paints relative to the Nifty 50 (illustrative)

children.text: The market's overall multiple is roughly where it was, but Konark's premium has shrunk from 2.6× to 2.0× the Nifty. The derating is specific to Konark or its industry, which points straight back to competition, growth and returns, not to a general market sell-off.
Putting Both Benchmarks Together

body.title: A peer and history check on screener.in
steps: Open the company page and scroll to the peer comparison table. Note the industry label it uses.
For each listed peer, check its business description and segment mix. Remove companies with different business models.
Add better peers you know from annual reports, earnings calls or offer documents.
Compare the remaining peers on sales growth, ROCE, margins and debt, not just P/E. Use the median multiple and exclude loss-makers.
In the chart section, select the P/E ratio (and price to book or EV/EBITDA where relevant) over 10 years. Note the median shown.
Identify distorted years, such as pandemic-affected earnings, one-off gains or a change from standalone to consolidated reporting, and discount them.
Ask what has changed since the historical median was set: competition, growth, returns, interest rates.
Only then decide whether today's discount or premium is justified, and cross-check with a DCF or reverse DCF.

body.label: screener.in
body.description: Every company page includes a peer comparison table and a chart section for plotting valuation ratios such as P/E over periods up to ten years or more, alongside ten years of financials.

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Median vs average
body.prompt: Five peers of a tyre company trade at P/Es of 14, 18, 21, 25, 90. What is the median P/E?
body.explanation: Sorted, the middle value is 21×. The average is 33.6×, pulled up by one outlier at 90×, probably a company with depressed earnings or a very different growth story. The median better represents a typical peer.

body.title: Implied price from true peers
body.prompt: The tyre company has EPS of ₹50. Using the peer median P/E from the previous question, what price does relative valuation imply, in ₹?
body.explanation: Implied price = 21 × ₹50 = ₹1,050. Using the 33.6× average instead would have implied ₹1,680, a very different answer from the same five peers.

body.title: Pick the best peer set
body.question: You are valuing a mid-sized Indian IT services company focused on banking clients in the US and Europe. Which peer set is most appropriate?
options: All companies in the "IT - Software" industry on screener.in
Other mid-sized IT services firms with a large banking and financial services client base, adjusted for differences in growth and margins
The five largest Indian IT services companies by market cap
Indian banks, since its clients are banks
body.explanation: True peers share the business model, client exposure, size and growth profile. The broad industry list mixes product, engineering and services companies. The largest firms differ in scale, stability and liquidity. Banks are its customers, not its peers.

body.title: Handling outliers
body.textWithBlank: When summarising a peer group's multiples, use the ___ rather than the average, so that one or two extreme values do not distort the benchmark.
body.explanation: The median is the middle value and is not pulled around by a single company at 90× or 5×.

body.title: The IT mid-cap at a ten-year low
body.scenario: Vivek, a Hyderabad-based investor, notices that a listed IT services mid-cap trades at 18× trailing earnings, against a ten-year median of 28× on its screener.in P/E chart. A stock tip channel says: "Lowest valuation in a decade. Mean reversion alone gives 55% upside." Reading the latest earnings call and annual report, Vivek finds that its largest client, 35% of revenue, has cut technology spending; new deal wins have slowed for four quarters; two senior leaders have left; and the company has cut its revenue growth guidance from 14% to 6%. The Nifty 50's P/E is close to its own ten-year median, and the 10-year G-sec yield is higher than during most of the company's high-multiple years.
body.prompt: Should Vivek expect the P/E to return to 28×? What should he do instead?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The history is no longer a fair benchmark. The ten-year median was set when the company was growing faster, with a healthier client base. Its growth guidance has fallen from 14% to 6%, which on its own justifies a much lower multiple.
2. Concentration risk has become real. A client providing 35% of revenue cutting spending raises both earnings risk and the required return.
3. The derating is company-specific. The Nifty P/E is near its median, so the fall from 28× to 18× is not a market-wide mood swing that will simply reverse.
4. Interest rates are higher. A higher risk-free rate lowers justified multiples across the market, so even an unchanged business would struggle to regain its old peak multiple.
5. "55% upside from mean reversion" assumes nothing has changed, when almost everything has.

What Vivek should do: compare the stock with a true peer set of IT services companies with similar size, client mix and current growth; run a reverse DCF to see what growth 18× implies; check whether the market is pricing in more decline than the evidence supports; and only then decide. 18× could be fair, cheap or still expensive, but the ten-year median cannot tell him which.

points: A relative valuation is only as reliable as its benchmark: true peers and relevant history.
Choose peers on business model, growth, returns, leverage, size and cycle position, not on an industry label.
Use the median peer multiple, exclude loss-makers and outliers, and justify any premium or discount with fundamentals.
screener.in's peer table and valuation charts are starting points. Refine the peer list and clean distorted years before drawing conclusions.
Historical bands assume the business, its growth, competition and interest rates are unchanged. Often they are not.
Relative P/E against the Nifty helps separate company-specific derating from market-wide moves.
